newsitem.title: TAIWAN: Taiwan says no change in president's Panama visit.
newsitem.headline: Taiwan says no change in president's Panama visit.

text.p: Taiwan said on Tuesday that President Lee Teng-hui would go ahead with a visit to Panama this year despite pressure from rival China.
"There is no change in the president's visit," said Stephen Chen, Lee's deputy secretary-general.
Lee has been invited by Panama -- one of Taiwan's only 30 diplomatic allies -- to attend a conference on the future of the Panama Canal in Panama City in September.
Chen's comment came after newspapers reported that United Nations Secretary-General Kofi Annan and heads of several U.N. organisations would boycott the conference if Lee attended.
The reports said China had tried to use the United Nations to apply pressure on Panama to withdraw the invitation to Lee.
Taiwan Foreign Minister John Chang said on state radio the United Nations had yet to confirm the reports, but it was not surprising for China to use the world body to pressure Panama.
China, which has viewed Taiwan as a rebel province since a civil war split them in 1949, has protested against Lee's trip, saying Taiwan has no right to attend international meetings.
Chang, who also said Lee would go ahead with his trip, said his ministry had received assurances from the Panama government that there would be no change in the invitation despite China's pressure.
Taiwan has contributed US$800,000 to help organise the September conference.

Earlier in March, Chang said Beijing had set up an ad hoc committee to deal with Panama's invitation for Lee, hoping that the central American nation would not only withdraw Lee's invitation but also would sever diplomatic ties with Taipei.
To counter the Chinese diplomatic campaign, Chang said he would visit several countries before June to solidify their ties with Taiwan. He declined to name the countries.
Chang has said he is confident that ties with other allies would remain unchanged despite Beijing's pressure.
Taiwan's biggest ally, South Africa, announced in November it would switch recognition to Beijing by the end of 1997.
